int utf8_next(const unsigned char *s, size_t n, uint32_t *cp) {
    if (n == 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    uint32_t cpv = s[0];

    if (cpv < 0x80) {
        *cp = cpv;
        return 1;
    }

    if (cpv < 0xC0) {
        /* Continuation byte in leading position */
        return -1;
    }

    if (cpv < 0xE0) {
        if (n < 2) {
            return -1;
        }
        if ((s[1] & 0xC0) != 0x80) {
            return -1;
        }
        cpv = ((cpv & 0x1F) << 6) | (s[1] & 0x3F);
        /* Overlong check: 2-byte form must encode >= 0x80 */
        if (cpv < 0x80) {
            return -1;
        }
        *cp = cpv;
        return 2;
    }

    if (cpv < 0xF0) {
        if (n < 3) {
            return -1;
        }
        if ((s[1] & 0xC0) != 0x80) {
            return -1;
        }
        if ((s[2] & 0xC0) != 0x80) {
            return -1;
        }
        cpv = ((cpv & 0x0F) << 12) | ((s[1] & 0x3F) << 6) | (s[2] & 0x3F);
        /* Overlong check: 3-byte form must encode >= 0x800 */
        if (cpv < 0x800) {
            return -1;
        }
        /* Surrogate range */
        if (cpv >= 0xD800 && cpv <= 0xDFFF) {
            return -1;
        }
        *cp = cpv;
        return 3;
    }

    if (cpv < 0xF8) {
        /* 4-byte form (and obsolete 5/6-byte forms rejected here) */
        if (n < 4) {
            return -1;
        }
        if ((s[1] & 0xC0) != 0x80) {
            return -1;
        }
        if ((s[2] & 0xC0) != 0x80) {
            return -1;
        }
        if ((s[3] & 0xC0) != 0x80) {
            return -1;
        }
        cpv = ((cpv & 0x07) << 18) | ((s[1] & 0x3F) << 12) |
              ((s[2] & 0x3F) << 6) | (s[3] & 0x3F);
        /* Overlong check: 4-byte form must encode >= 0x10000 */
        if (cpv < 0x10000) {
            return -1;
        }
        /* Above maximum code point */
        if (cpv > 0x10FFFF) {
            return -1;
        }
        *cp = cpv;
        return 4;
    }

    /* 0xF8 and above: obsolete 5- and 6-byte forms */
    return -1;
}

               | (uint32_t)(s[1] & 0x3f);

               | (uint32_t)(s[2] & 0x3f);
        /* Reject overlong (U+0080..U+07FF must use at most 2 bytes) */
        if (cp_val < 0x80) {
            return -1;
        }
        /* Reject surrogate code points */
        if (cp_val >= 0xD800 && cp_val <= 0xDFFF) {
            return -1;
        }
        num_bytes = 3;
    } else if ((s[0] & 0xf8) == 0xf0) {
        /* 4-byte sequence: 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx */
        if (n < 4) {
            return -1;

        for (i = 1; i < 4; i++) {

               | (uint32_t)(s[1] & 0x3f) << 12
               | (uint32_t)(s[2] & 0x3f) << 6
               | (uint32_t)(s[3] & 0x3f);
        /* Reject overlong (U+0800..U+FFFF must use at most 3 bytes) */
        if (cp_val < 0x800) {

        if (cp_val > 0x10FFFF) {

        }

    } else {

         * or invalid lead byte (111110xx / 111111xx / 1xxxxxxx).
         * These correspond to the obsolete 5- and 6-byte forms
         * and other malformed lead bytes. */
        return -1;
    }

def clone(obj):
    id_map = {}

    def _clone(obj):
        if isinstance(obj, dict):
            if id(obj) in id_map:
                return id_map[id(obj)]
            new = {}
            id_map[id(obj)] = new
            for k, v in obj.items():
                new[k] = _clone(v)
            return new
        elif isinstance(obj, (list, tuple)):
            if id(obj) in id_map:
                return id_map[id(obj)]
            new = type(obj)([None] * len(obj))
            id_map[id(obj)] = new
            for i, v in enumerate(obj):
                new[i] = _clone(v)
            return new
        else:
            return obj

    return _clone(obj)

Implement in bash: `csv_to_tsv <file>`. Converts an RFC-4180 CSV file to TSV on stdout. Each CSV record becomes one output line, fields joined by a single tab. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, often referred to simply as MIT, stands not merely as an educational institution but as a gravitational center for the intellectual history of artificial intelligence, a place where the abstract dreams of computing were forged into the tangible realities of modern machine learning, robotics, and cognitive science. To understand the profound influence of MIT on AI research is to trace the very lineage of the field itself, beginning in the late 1950s when the term "artificial intelligence" was coined at the seminal Dartmouth Conference, an event heavily influenced by the academic circles surrounding MIT, particularly through the contributions of Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy, though it was at MIT that the first dedicated AI laboratory was established, marking the beginning of a sustained, institutionalized effort to create machines that could think, learn, and perceive. This early era, often romanticized as the "golden age" of AI, was characterized by an optimistic belief that human intelligence could be decomposed into logical rules and algorithms, a perspective that dominated the MIT AI Lab under the leadership of Minsky and Seymour Papert, whose work on perceptrons and the limitations of single-layer neural networks, while initially casting a shadow over connectionist approaches, inadvertently spurred the development of symbolic AI and expert systems that would dominate the field for decades. However, the true genius of MIT’s contribution lies not just in its early successes but in its ability to pivot, adapt, and eventually lead the resurgence of neural networks and deep learning, a transformation that was not immediate but rather a slow, painful, and ultimately triumphant evolution through the "AI winters" that saw funding dry up and interest wane, periods during which MIT researchers continued to explore the fundamental boundaries of computation, perception, and interaction, laying the groundwork for the modern era. The transition from the old AI Lab to the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) in 2003, through the merger with the Laboratory for Computer Science, symbolized a broader integration of AI into the fabric of computer science, reflecting a shift from viewing AI as a separate, esoteric discipline to recognizing it as a fundamental component of computing itself. This institutional evolution mirrored the technical shift towards data-driven methods, as the availability of large datasets and increased computational power allowed MIT researchers to revive and refine neural network architectures, leading to groundbreaking work in computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. Today, MIT’s influence on AI is pervasive and multifaceted, extending far beyond the confines of its campus to shape the global landscape of technology, ethics, and policy. In this way, MIT’s influence on AI is not just a historical footnote but a living, evolving force that continues to shape the direction of the field and the world. void itoa(int value, char *buf) {

        is_negative = 1;
        *p++ = '-';
        // Handle INT_MIN specially to avoid overflow when negating
        *p++ = '1';
        *p++ = '2';
        *p++ = '7';
        *p++ = '6';

        *p++ = '9';
        *p++ = '2';
        *p++ = '3';
        *p++ = '4';
        *p++ = '8';
        *p++ = '\0';
        return;

    if (value < 0) {
        is_negative = 1;
        value = -value;
    }

    // Generate digits in reverse order
    while (value != 0) {
        *p++ = (value % 10) + '0';
        value /= 10;

        buf[end] = temp;

void trim(char *s) {
    if (s == NULL) return;

    // Find the first non-whitespace character
    char *start = s;
    while (*start == ' ' || *start == '\t' || *start == '\n') {
        start++;
    }

    // If the string is all whitespace, make it empty
    if (*start == '\0') {
        *s = '\0';
        return;
    }

    // Find the last non-whitespace character
    char *end = s + strlen(s) - 1;
    while (end > start && (*end == ' ' || *end == '\t' || *end == '\n')) {
        end--;
    }

    // Move the trimmed substring to the beginning of the original string
    if (start != s) {
        memmove(s, start, (size_t)(end - start + 1));
    }

    // Null-terminate the string
    *(s + (end - start + 1)) = '\0';
}

    /* Move the trimmed substring to the beginning of the buffer */
    if (start != s) {
        size_t len = (size_t)(end - start + 1);
        memmove(s, start, len);
    }

    /* Null-terminate */
    s[end - start + 1] = '\0';
}

int cmp_desc(const void *a, const void *b) {
    const int ia = *(const int *)a;
    const int ib = *(const int *)b;

    if (ia > 0 && ib < 0) return 1;
    if (ia < 0 && ib > 0) return -1;

    if (*p == '-') {
        sign = -1;
        p++;
    } else if (*p == '+') {
        sign = 1;
        p++;

        return -1;

        p++;

    if (*p != '\0') {
        return -1;
    }

    *out = sign * value;
    return 0;
}

#include <stddef.h>

static int glob_match_tail(const char *pat, const char *str) {
    while (*str != '\0' && *pat != '*') {
        if (*pat != '?' && *pat != *str) {
            return 0;
        }
        pat++;
        str++;
    }
    while (*pat == '*') {
        pat++;
    }
    return (*pat == '\0') ? 1 : 0;
}

int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str) {
    while (*pat != '\0') {
        if (*pat == '*') {
            if (*(pat + 1) == '\0') {
                return 1;
            }
            do {
                if (glob_match_tail(pat + 1, str)) {
                    return 1;
                }
                str++;
            } while (*str != '\0');
            return 0;
        } else if (*pat != '?' && *pat != *str) {
            return 0;
        } else {
            pat++;
            str++;
        }
    }
    return (*str == '\0') ? 1 : 0;
}

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <ctype.h>
#include <math.h>

double rpn_eval(const char *expr) {
    double stack[1024];
    int top = -1;
    
    const char *ptr = expr;
    
    while (*ptr) {
        // Skip whitespace
        while (*ptr == ' ')
            ptr++;
        
        if (*ptr == '\0')
            break;
        
        // Check if it's a number
        if (isdigit(*ptr) || *ptr == '.' || *ptr == '-') {
            // Parse number
            char num_str[64];
            int i = 0;
            while (*ptr && (*ptr != ' ')) {
                if (i < 63)
                    num_str[i++] = *ptr;
                ptr++;
            }
            num_str[i] = '\0';
            stack[++top] = atof(num_str);
        } else {
            // It's an operator
            char op = *ptr;
            ptr++;
            
            double b = stack[top--];
            double a = stack[top--];
            
            switch (op) {
                case '+':
                    stack[++top] = a + b;
                    break;
                case '-':
                    stack[++top] = a - b;
                    break;
                case '*':
                    stack[++top] = a * b;
                    break;
                case '/':
                    stack[++top] = a / b;
                    break;
            }
        }
    }
    
    return stack[0];
}

        if (current_idx == idx) {
            found = 1;

        if (*p == '"') {
            // Quoted field
            p++; // skip opening quote
            while (*p != '\0') {
                if (*p == '"') {
                    if (*(p + 1) == '"') {
                        p += 2; // escaped quote
                    } else {
                        p++; // closing quote
                        break;
                    }
                } else {
                    p++;
                }
            }
            if (*p == ',') {
                p++; // skip comma
            }
        } else {
            // Unquoted field

            }

                p++; // skip comma
            }
        }

    }

    if (!found) {
        return -1;
    }

    size_t out_len = 0;
    int is_quoted = (*p == '"');

    if (is_quoted) {
        p++; // skip opening quote
        while (*p != '\0') {
            if (*p == '"') {
                if (*(p + 1) == '"') {
                    if (out_len + 1 < cap) {
                        out[out_len++] = '"';
                    }
                    p += 2;
                } else {
                    // Closing quote
                    p++; // skip closing quote
                    break;
                }
            } else {
                if (out_len + 1 < cap) {
                    out[out_len++] = *p;
                }
                p++;
            }
        }
        // Skip trailing comma if present
        if (*p == ',') {
            p++;
        }
    } else {
        while (*p != ',' && *p != '\0') {
            if (out_len + 1 < cap) {
                out[out_len++] = *p;

            p++;
        }

        }

    *   **What changed:** RHEL 10 fully supports NFS with Transport Layer Security (TLS) for RPC traffic, utilizing kernel TLS (kTLS), which is available as a Technology Preview.
    *   **Why it matters:** This enhances security by ensuring encrypted communication between NFS clients and servers, protecting data in transit.

*   **ReaR NFS/SSHFS URL parsing for IPv6**
    *   **What changed:** The ReaR backup and restore tool now correctly parses `nfs://` (and `sshfs://`) URLs containing IPv6 addresses enclosed in square brackets (e.g., `nfs://[2001:db8...]/...`) without interpreting the brackets as shell metacharacters.
    *   **Why it matters:** Fixes a bug that caused ReaR to abort prematurely when using IPv6 addresses in NFS backup/output URLs, removing the need for manual workaround escaping.

*   **Increased maximum NFS read/write buffer sizes**
    *   **What changed:** The default maximum values for `rsize` (read) and `wsize` (write) mount options are now 1,048,576 bytes (1 MB) for both client and server.
    *   **Why it matters:** Allows for larger data transfers per operation, which can improve NFS throughput and performance by reducing the number of round-trips required for large file operations.

*   **FS-Cache integration for NFS client-side caching**
    *   **What changed:** The documentation details the use of FS-Cache with the `cachefiles` backend to enable transparent client-side caching for NFS mounts.
    *   **Why it matters:** Improves NFS performance by satisfying read requests locally from the cache, reducing network traffic and lowering server load, though it requires specific filesystem backends (XFS, ext3, ext4) and may introduce latency trade-offs.

void reverse_string(char *s) {
	if (!s)
		return;
	size_t len = 0;
	while (s[len] != '\0')
		len++;
	size_t i = 0;
	size_t j = len - 1;
	while (i < j) {
		char tmp = s[i];
		s[i] = s[j];
		s[j] = tmp;
		i++;

}

#include <ctype.h>

int parse_csv_ints(const char *s, int *out, int max) {
    int count = 0;
    const char *p = s;

    while (*p && count < max) {
        int sign = 1;
        // Skip whitespace (optional, but robust)
        while (isspace((unsigned char)*p)) p++;
        if (*p == '-') {
            sign = -1;
            p++;
        } else if (*p == '+') {
            p++;
        }

        if (!isdigit((unsigned char)*p)) {
            // Not a valid integer start, skip to next comma or end
            while (*p && *p != ',') p++;
            if (*p == ',') p++;
            continue;
        }

        int val = 0;
        int overflow = 0;
        while (isdigit((unsigned char)*p)) {
            int digit = *p - '0';
            // Simple overflow check for int
            if (val > (INT_MAX - digit) / 10) {
                overflow = 1;
                break;
            }
            val = val * 10 + digit;
            p++;
        }

        if (overflow) {
            // Handle overflow by clamping or skipping; here we skip
            while (*p && *p != ',') p++;
            if (*p == ',') p++;
            continue;
        }

        out[count++] = sign * val;

        // Skip to next comma
        while (*p && *p != ',') p++;
        if (*p == ',') p++;
    }

    return count;
}

csv_col() {
    local col_name="$1"
    local header
    IFS= read -r header
    if [ -z "$header" ]; then
        return 0
    fi

    # Find column index (0-based)
    local col_idx=-1
    local IFS=','
    local i=0
    for h in $header; do
        # Trim whitespace and quotes if necessary
        h=$(echo "$h" | sed 's/^[[:space:]]*//;s/[[:space:]]*$//;s/^"//;s/"$//')
        if [ "$h" = "$col_name" ]; then
            col_idx=$i
            break
        fi
        ((i++))
    done

    if [ $col_idx -eq -1 ]; then
        return 1
    fi

    # Process remaining lines
    local line
    while IFS= read -r line; do
        if [ -z "$line" ]; then
            continue
        fi
        
        # Use awk to extract the column, handling CSV properly is complex, 
        # but for a standard bash one-liner we can use awk with comma delimiter.
        # This assumes no commas within quoted fields for simplicity, 
        # or uses a basic split. For robust CSV, awk with FPAT is better (GNU awk).
        echo "$line" | awk -v col="$((col_idx + 1))" 'BEGIN{FPAT="([^,]*)|(\"[^\"]*\")"} {print $col}'
    done
}

find_dupes() {
    local dir="${1:-.}"
    if [ ! -d "$dir" ]; then
        echo "Error: '$dir' is not a directory" >&2
        return 1
    fi

    # Find all regular files, compute MD5, store in associative array
    # Using BSD md5 -r output format: "MD5 (filename) = hash"
    # We need to handle filenames with spaces/newlines safely.
    
    declare -A hash_map
    
    # Use find with -exec to handle filenames safely
    # We collect: hash<TAB>filepath
    while IFS= read -r -d '' line; do
        # line format from md5 -r: "MD5 (filepath) = hash" or "MD5 filepath = hash"
        # macOS md5 -r output: "MD5 (path) = hash"
        # Extract hash: it's the part after "= "
        local hash="${line##*= }"
        hash="${hash%"${hash##*[![:space:]]}"}" # trim trailing space
        # Extract path: between "( " and " )" or handle if no parens
        local filepath="${line#MD5 (}"
        filepath="${filepath%%)" = *}"
        # If no parens (older format?), try:
        if [[ "$filepath" == *"MD5"* ]]; then
            # Fallback for non-paren format: "MD5 path = hash"
            filepath="${line#MD5 }"
            filepath="${filepath%% = *}"
        fi
        # Remove any residual spaces
        filepath="${filepath#"${filepath%%[![:space:]]*}"}"
        
        # Add to map: collect paths for each hash
        if [[ -n "$hash" ]]; then
            if [[ -v hash_map["$hash"] ]]; then
                hash_map["$hash"]+=$'\n'"$filepath"
            else
                hash_map["$hash"]="$filepath"
            fi
        fi
    done < <(find "$dir" -type f -print0 | xargs -0 md5 -r 2>/dev/null)

    # Process groups
    local output_lines=()
    for hash in "${!hash_map[@]}"; do
        local paths_str="${hash_map[$hash]}"
        # Count files
        local count=0
        while IFS= read -r p; do
            [ -z "$p" ] && continue
            ((count++))
        done <<< "$paths_str"
        
        if (( count >= 2 )); then
            # Sort paths within group
            local sorted_paths
            sorted_paths=$(echo "$paths_str" | sort)
            # Convert to space-separated string
            local line
            line=$(echo "$sorted_paths" | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ *$//')
            output_lines+=("$line")
        fi
    done

    # Sort groups by first path
    if (( ${#output_lines[@]} > 0 )); then
        printf '%s\n' "${output_lines[@]}" | sort -t' ' -k1,1
    fi
}

backup_rotate() {
    local dir="$1"
    local keep="$2"
    local files
    local count
    local i=0

    # Check if directory exists
    if [[ ! -d "$dir" ]]; then
        return 1
    fi

    # Find all matching files, sorted lexicographically (which corresponds to newest first for YYYYMMDD formats, but we need to be careful)
    # The problem states "newest = lexicographically greatest names"
    # So we sort them in reverse order (newest first)
    
    # Get list of matching files
    files=()
    while IFS= read -r file; do
        # Extract just the filename
        local fname
        fname="$(basename "$file")"
        files+=("$fname")
    done < <(find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -name 'backup-*.tar.gz' -type f | sort -r)

    count=${#files[@]}

    # If less than or equal to keep, do nothing
    if (( count <= keep )); then
        return 0
    fi

    # Calculate how many to delete
    local delete_count=$(( count - keep ))

    # The files array is sorted with newest first (reverse lex order)
    # We want to delete the oldest ones first
    # Oldest are at the end of the reversed list
    # So we iterate from index 'keep' to 'count - 1'
    
    while (( i < delete_count )); do
        local file_index=$(( keep + i ))
        local fname="${files[$file_index]}"
        echo "$fname"
        rm -f "$dir/$fname"
        ((i++))
    done
}

void reverse_string(char *s) {
    if (s == NULL) return;
    char *start = s;
    char *end = s;
    while (*end != '\0') end++;
    end--;
    while (start < end) {
        char tmp = *start;
        *start = *end;
        *end = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;

void trim(char *s) {
    char *end;

    while (isspace((unsigned char)*s)) {
        s++;

int atoi_strict(const char *s, int *out) {
    if (s == NULL || out == NULL) return -1;
    const char *p = s;
    int neg = 0;
    if (*p == '-') {
        neg = 1;
        ++p;
    } else if (*p == '+') {
        ++p;
    }
    if (*p == '\0') return -1;
    long val = 0;
    while (*p >= '0' && *p <= '9') {
        val = val * 10 + (*p - '0');
        ++p;
    }
    if (*p != '\0') return -1;
    if (neg) val = -val;
    *out = (int)val;
    return 0;
}

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap) {
    if (line == NULL || out == NULL || cap == 0 || idx < 0)
        return -1;

    int field = 0;
    int in_quotes = 0;
    size_t len = 0;

    for (const char *p = line; ; ++p) {
        if (*p == '\0') {
            if (field == idx) {
                if (len >= cap - 1)
                    len = cap - 1;
                out[len] = '\0';
                return (int)len;
            }
            return -1;
        }

        if (in_quotes) {
            if (*p == '"') {
                if (p[1] == '"') {
                    if (len < cap - 1)
                        out[len++] = '"';
                    ++p;
                } else {
                    in_quotes = 0;
                }
            } else {
                if (len < cap - 1)
                    out[len++] = *p;
            }
        } else {
            if (*p == '"') {
                in_quotes = 1;
            } else if (*p == ',') {
                if (field == idx) {
                    if (len >= cap - 1)
                        len = cap - 1;
                    out[len] = '\0';
                    return (int)len;
                }
                ++field;
            } else {
                if (len < cap - 1)
                    out[len++] = *p;
            }
        }
    }
}

Returns None if the graph has a cycle (including self-dependencies). Nodes mentioned only as dependencies are included.

trial 1 (temp 0.7) — fail — AssertionError: ['app', 'lib', 'base']
def topological_sort(deps):
    # Build full graph including nodes that appear only as dependencies
    graph = {}
    for node, dependencies in deps.items():
        graph.setdefault(node, [])
        for dep in dependencies:
            graph.setdefault(dep, [])
            graph[node].append(dep)

    # Kahn's algorithm
    in_degree = {node: 0 for node in graph}
    for node, dependencies in graph.items():
        for dep in dependencies:
            in_degree[dep] += 1

    queue = [node for node in graph if in_degree[node] == 0]
    result = []

    while queue:
        node = queue.pop(0)
        result.append(node)
        for dep in graph[node]:
            in_degree[dep] -= 1
            if in_degree[dep] == 0:
                queue.append(dep)

    if len(result) != len(graph):
        return None
    return result
trial 2 (temp 0.7) — fail — AssertionError: ['app', 'lib', 'base']
def topological_sort(deps):
    graph = {}
    for node, dependencies in deps.items():
        graph.setdefault(node, [])
        for dep in dependencies:
            graph.setdefault(dep, [])
            graph[node].append(dep)

    state = {}
    order = []

    def visit(node):
        if state.get(node) == 1:
            return
        if state.get(node) == 2:
            return
        state[node] = 1
        for dep in graph[node]:
            visit(dep)
        state[node] = 2
        order.append(node)

    for node in graph:
        if node not in state:
            visit(node)

    if len(order) != len(graph):
        return None
    order.reverse()
    return order

    diffs = []

    def compare(x, y, path):
        if type(x) is not type(y):
            diffs.append(path)
            return
        if isinstance(x, dict):

            for k in sorted(keys):

                    diffs.append(path + "." + k)
                else:

        elif isinstance(x, list):
            if x != y:

top_errors() {
    local logfile="$1" n="$2"
    grep -o 'ERROR: .*' "$logfile" \
    | sed 's/^ERROR: //' \

}

void trim(char *s) {

        s++;

    // If string is empty after removing leading whitespace, return

    // Remove trailing whitespace

#include <stdbool.h>

int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str) {
    bool match[2][256];
    match[0][0] = true;

    for (int i = 1; i <= 256; i++) {
        match[0][i] = false;
    }

    while (*pat) {
        bool next[2][256];
        for (int i = 0; i <= 256; i++) {
            next[0][i] = false;
            next[1][i] = false;
        }

        if (*pat == '*') {
            for (int i = 0; i <= 256; i++) {
                next[0][i] = match[0][i] || match[1][i];
            }
            pat++;
        } else if (*pat == '?') {
            for (int i = 0; i < 256; i++) {
                next[1][i + 1] = match[0][i];
            }
            pat++;
        } else {
            for (int i = 0; i < 256; i++) {
                if (match[0][i] && str[i] == *pat) {
                    next[1][i + 1] = true;
                }
            }
            pat++;
        }

        for (int i = 0; i <= 256; i++) {
            match[0][i] = next[0][i];
            match[1][i] = next[1][i];
        }
    }

    return match[0][256 - 1];
}

#include <string.h>

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap) {
    int field_idx = 0;
    int in_quote = 0;
    int out_idx = 0;
    int prev_quote = 0;

    while (*line) {
        if (in_quote) {
            if (*line == '"' && prev_quote) {
                prev_quote = 0;
                if (out_idx < cap - 1) {
                    out[out_idx++] = '"';
                }
            } else if (*line == '"') {
                prev_quote = 1;
            } else {
                prev_quote = 0;
                if (out_idx < cap - 1) {
                    out[out_idx++] = *line;
                }
            }
        } else {
            if (*line == ',') {
                field_idx++;
                if (field_idx == idx) {
                    out[out_idx] = '\0';
                    return out_idx;
                }
                out_idx = 0;
            } else if (*line == '"') {
                in_quote = 1;
            } else if (field_idx == idx) {
                if (out_idx < cap - 1) {
                    out[out_idx++] = *line;
                }
            }
        }
        line++;
    }

    if (field_idx == idx) {
        out[out_idx] = '\0';
        return out_idx;
    }

    return -1;
}

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap) {
    bool in_quote = false;
    bool field_started = false;
    int field_idx = 0;
    size_t out_idx = 0;

    for (const char *c = line; *c; ++c) {
        if (!field_started) {
            if (*c == '\"') {
                in_quote = true;
                field_started = true;
            } else if (*c == ',') {
                ++field_idx;
            } else if (*c != ' ' && *c != '\t') {
                field_started = true;
            }
        } else {
            if (in_quote) {
                if (*c == '\"') {
                    in_quote = false;
                } else {
                    if (out_idx < cap - 1 && field_idx == idx) {
                        out[out_idx++] = *c;
                    }
                }
            } else {
                if (*c == ',') {
                    field_started = false;
                    in_quote = false;
                    ++field_idx;
                    if (field_idx == idx) {
                        out[out_idx] = '\0';
                        return out_idx;
                    }
                } else if (*c == '\"') {
                    in_quote = true;
                } else if (out_idx < cap - 1 && field_idx == idx) {
                    out[out_idx++] = *c;
                }
            }
        }
    }

    if (field_idx == idx) {
        out[out_idx] = '\0';
        return out_idx;
    } else {
        return -1;
    }
}

#include <string.h>

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap) {
    int field_idx = 0;
    int in_quote = 0;
    int out_idx = 0;
    int prev_quote = 0;

    for (const char *p = line; *p; p++) {
        if (in_quote) {
            if (*p == '"' && prev_quote) {
                out[out_idx++] = '"';
                prev_quote = 0;
            } else if (*p == '"') {
                prev_quote = 1;
            } else {
                out[out_idx++] = *p;
                prev_quote = 0;
            }
        } else {
            if (*p == ',') {
                if (field_idx == idx) {
                    out[out_idx] = '\0';
                    return out_idx;
                }
                field_idx++;
            } else if (*p == '"') {
                in_quote = 1;
                prev_quote = 0;
            } else {
                if (field_idx == idx) {
                    out[out_idx++] = *p;
                }
            }
        }

        if (out_idx >= cap - 1) {
            out[cap - 1] = '\0';
            return -1;
        }
    }

    if (in_quote) {
        return -1;
    }

    if (field_idx == idx) {
        out[out_idx] = '\0';
        return out_idx;
    }

    return -1;
}

backup_rotate() {
  local dir="$1"
  local keep="$2"
  local files=("$dir"/backup-*.tar.gz)
  if (( ${#files[@]} <= keep )); then
    return
  fi
  local sorted_files=($(printf '%s\n' "${files[@]}" | sort -r))
  local to_delete=("${sorted_files[@]:keep}")
  for file in "${to_delete[@]}"; do
    echo "${file##*/}"
    rm "$file"
  done
}

backup_rotate() {
  local dir=$1
  local keep=$2
  local files=("$dir"/backup-*.tar.gz)
  local delete_count=$(( ${#files[@]} - keep ))
  if (( delete_count > 0 )); then
    printf '%s\n' "${files[@]:0:delete_count}" | sort -r | while read -r file; do
      rm "$file"
      echo "${file##*/}"
    done
  fi
}

To understand the profound influence of MIT on AI research and discoveries is to trace the very arc of the discipline's history, from its theoretical infancy in the mid-twentieth century to its current status as a ubiquitous force reshaping every facet of human existence, from healthcare and transportation to finance and the arts. The story begins not with a single breakthrough, but with a unique institutional culture that prioritizes the intersection of rigorous theoretical mathematics, practical engineering, and bold, often radical, speculation about the future of human-machine interaction. In the late 1940s and early 1950s, while the world was still grappling with the implications of the atomic age, a small group of visionaries at MIT, including figures like Norbert Wiener, who coined the term "cybernetics," began to lay the groundwork for understanding systems that could learn, adapt, and process information in ways that mimicked biological intelligence. This early period was characterized by a distinct lack of boundaries between disciplines; the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, and the nascent fields of cognitive science were not siloed but were instead deeply intertwined, fostering an environment where a mathematician could collaborate with a psychologist to solve problems that neither could tackle alone. Under the leadership of figures such as Rodney Brooks, who championed the idea of "subsumption architecture" and embodied robotics, and later, the visionary work of researchers like Patrick Winston and Marvin Minsky, MIT shifted the focus from purely symbolic, logic-based reasoning to more connectionist and embodied approaches, recognizing that true intelligence might emerge from the interaction between an agent and its environment rather than from abstract rule sets. This shift laid the groundwork for the deep learning revolution that would explode in the 2010s, a revolution that was significantly accelerated by the work of MIT researchers who developed the theoretical underpinnings and practical algorithms that made training massive neural networks feasible. The influence of MIT on the specific architecture of modern AI cannot be overstated; the backpropagation algorithm, the fundamental engine of deep learning, was refined and popularized by researchers at the institute, while the development of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and the Transformer architecture, which powers today's large language models, owes a significant debt to the collaborative, open-source culture fostered within MIT's labs. Furthermore, MIT has been instrumental in addressing the ethical and societal implications of AI, recognizing early on that the power to create intelligent systems carries with it a profound responsibility to ensure those systems are fair, transparent, and aligned with human values. This ethical dimension is not an afterthought at MIT but is woven into the fabric of the research itself, with projects ranging from algorithmic fairness and bias detection to the development of privacy-preserving machine learning techniques that allow for data analysis without compromising individual privacy. void itoa(int value, char *buf) {
    int i = 0;
    unsigned int uval;
    int is_neg = 0;

    if (value == INT_MIN) {
        // Handle INT_MIN separately to avoid overflow when negating
        // INT_MIN is -2147483648
        buf[i++] = '-';
        uval = (unsigned int)INT_MAX + 1U; // Which is 2147483648
    } else if (value < 0) {
        buf[i++] = '-';
        uval = (unsigned int)(-value);
    } else {
        uval = (unsigned int)value;
    }

    if (uval == 0) {
        buf[i++] = '0';
    } else {
        while (uval > 0) {
            buf[i++] = '0' + (uval % 10);
            uval /= 10;
        }
    }

    buf[i] = '\0';

    // Reverse the string
    int start = 0;
    int end = i - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        char tmp = buf[start];
        buf[start] = buf[end];
        buf[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

#include <string.h>
#include <ctype.h>

void trim(char *s) {
    if (s == NULL) return;

    char *start = s;
    char *end;

    // Strip leading whitespace
    while (isspace(*start)) {
        start++;
    }

    // If string is all whitespace or empty
    if (*start == '\0') {
        *start = '\0';
        return;
    }

    // Find end of string
    end = start + strlen(start) - 1;

    // Strip trailing whitespace
    while (end > start && isspace(*end)) {
        end--;
    }

    // Move trimmed content to the beginning
    size_t len = end - start + 1;
    memmove(s, start, len);
    s[len] = '\0';
}

def csv_column_sum(path, col):
    import csv
    total = 0.0
    with open(path, 'r', newline='') as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        fieldnames = reader.fieldnames
        if col < 0 or col >= len(fieldnames):
            return 0.0
        col_name = fieldnames[col]
        for row in reader:
            try:
                value = float(row[col_name])
                total += value
            except (ValueError, KeyError):
                continue
    return total

#include <stdbool.h>

int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str) {
    const char *s = str;
    const char *p = pat;
    const char *star = NULL;
    const char *match = NULL;

    while (*s) {
        if (*p == *s) {
            p++;
            s++;
        } else if (*p == '?') {
            p++;
            s++;
        } else if (*p == '*') {
            star = p++;
            match = s;
        } else if (star) {
            p = star + 1;
            s = ++match;
        } else {
            return 0;
        }
    }

    while (*p == '*') {
        p++;
    }

    return *p == '\0';
}

def json_diff(a, b, path=""):
    """
    Compares two JSON-like structures and returns a sorted list of dotted key paths where they differ.
    """
    diffs = []

    if type(a) != type(b):

find_dupes() {
  local dir="${1:-.}"
  
  [ -d "$dir" ] || return 1

  # Collect MD5 hashes and paths for regular files
  # Using BSD 'md5 -r' format: <hash>  <path>
  # We need to handle spaces in filenames correctly
  local temp_file
  temp_file=$(mktemp)
  trap "rm -f '$temp_file'" EXIT

  find "$dir" -type f -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
    # Get md5 hash using BSD md5
    hash=$(md5 -r "$file" 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}')
    if [ -n "$hash" ]; then
      # Store hash and path separated by a null byte to handle spaces/special chars
      printf '%s\t%s\0' "$hash" "$file"
    fi
  done > "$temp_file"

  # Process the collected data
  # Sort by hash, then by path
  # Use a custom sort key: hash (field 1) then path (field 2)
  # Since we used tabs as delimiters, we can sort by hash, then path
  
  # Re-read and group
  declare -A groups
  
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r hash path; do
    if [ -n "$hash" ]; then
      if [ -z "${groups[$hash]}" ]; then
        groups[$hash]="$path"
      else
        groups[$hash]="${groups[$hash]}"$'\n'"$path"
      fi
    fi
  done < "$temp_file"

  # Iterate over hashes with multiple files
  for hash in "${!groups[@]}"; do
    files="${groups[$hash]}"
    count=$(echo "$files" | wc -l)
    
    if [ "$count" -ge 2 ]; then
      # Sort the paths within the group and join with space
      sorted_paths=$(echo "$files" | sort | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')
      # We need to store this group with its first path for final sorting
      first_path=$(echo "$files" | sort | head -n 1)
      printf '%s\t%s\n' "$first_path" "$sorted_paths"
    fi
  done | sort -t$'\t' -k1,1 | cut -f2
}

    # We collect name and md5 hash, then group by hash

    local tmpfile=$(mktemp)
    local tmpgroup=$(mktemp)
    
    # Cleanup on exit
    trap "rm -f $tmpfile $tmpgroup" EXIT

    # Iterate over files, compute md5, store "hash  path"

        # To ensure deterministic sorting, we store the path exactly as returned by find.

Massachusetts Institute of Technology, commonly known as MIT, stands as one of the most influential institutions in the advancement of artificial intelligence research, consistently pushing the boundaries of what machines can accomplish and how humans interact with intelligent systems. Since the dawn of computing, MIT has been at the forefront of technological innovation, fostering an environment where groundbreaking discoveries in AI are not merely anticipated but regularly realized. The institution's influence on AI research began in the 1950s and 1960s when pioneering computer scientists like Marvin Minsky, who co-founded MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1959, established foundational theories about machine learning and cognitive science. This laboratory, later renamed the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), became a crucible for some of the most significant AI breakthroughs in history, including early work on neural networks, expert systems, and natural language processing. The interdisciplinary nature of MIT's research culture has proven instrumental in AI development, as researchers there frequently collaborate across departments including brain and cognitive sciences, electrical engineering, and mathematics, creating a holistic approach to understanding intelligence itself. This cross-pollination of ideas has led to innovations that might not emerge in more siloed academic environments, such as the development of reinforcement learning algorithms that draw from both computational theory and neuroscience insights.

One of MIT's most notable contributions to AI research involves its role in developing core technologies that underpin modern artificial intelligence systems. The institution has been instrumental in advancing machine learning techniques, particularly through the work of researchers like Yoshua Bengio, who spent significant time at MIT before his famous tenure at the University of Montreal. MIT researchers were among the first to explore deep learning architectures, contributing to the theoretical frameworks that made today's neural networks possible. The Media Lab, another innovative MIT initiative, has fostered unconventional approaches to AI development, encouraging research into affective computing, which focuses on machines' ability to recognize and respond to human emotions. This work has profound implications for human-computer interaction, robotics, and personalized AI systems that can adapt to individual user needs and preferences. Additionally, MIT's Robotics Lab has developed autonomous systems that demonstrate remarkable dexterity and adaptability, from surgical robots that can perform complex procedures to autonomous vehicles that navigate real-world environments with increasing sophistication.

The influence of MIT extends beyond individual research projects to shaping the very culture and methodology of AI research itself. The institution's emphasis on open-source collaboration and knowledge sharing has helped establish norms within the AI community that prioritize collective progress over proprietary secrecy. This approach has accelerated the pace of discovery, as researchers worldwide can build upon MIT's innovations rather than starting from scratch. The MIT Press has published countless influential texts on artificial intelligence, serving as a primary disseminator of cutting-edge research and theoretical frameworks. Furthermore, MIT's annual conferences and workshops, such as the Theory and Practice of Logic Programming and numerous AI-focused symposiums, provide essential venues for researchers to share findings and debate emerging trends. The institution's graduate programs in artificial intelligence have trained thousands of researchers who have gone on to lead AI initiatives at tech companies, government agencies, and universities around the world, creating a global network of influence that amplifies MIT's impact exponentially.

MIT's approach to AI ethics and governance represents another crucial aspect of its influence on the field. As AI systems become increasingly powerful and pervasive, concerns about their societal implications have grown correspondingly. MIT has taken a leadership role in addressing these challenges through initiatives like the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing, which integrates technical excellence with ethical considerations and social responsibility. Researchers at MIT have pioneered frameworks for algorithmic fairness, helping ensure that AI systems do not perpetuate existing biases or discriminate against marginalized groups. Work on explainable AI (XAI) has been significantly advanced through MIT research, addressing the critical need for transparency in automated decision-making systems that affect everything from medical diagnoses to criminal justice outcomes. The institution's efforts in AI safety research have contributed to developing techniques that allow humans to better understand and control AI behavior, which is becoming increasingly important as systems approach human-level intelligence in specific domains.

The economic and industrial impact of MIT's AI research cannot be overstated. Similarly, advances in computer vision, natural language processing, and autonomous systems developed at MIT have been commercialized by major technology companies, generating billions in economic value while improving countless aspects of daily life. The startup ecosystem surrounding MIT, particularly through the MIT Innovation Initiative, has spawned numerous AI-focused companies that continue to drive technological progress. Companies like Akamai Technologies, whose content delivery networks rely heavily on AI optimization, and countless others emerged from MIT's entrepreneurial culture, demonstrating how academic research translates into real-world applications that benefit society broadly.

Looking toward the future, MIT's influence on AI research continues to grow as the institution invests heavily in next-generation technologies and emerging research areas. Researchers there are exploring how quantum algorithms might accelerate machine learning processes and solve optimization problems that currently require impractical amounts of time. Additionally, MIT's work on embodied AI, which focuses on developing intelligent systems that learn through physical interaction with their environment, represents a paradigm shift toward more robust and generalizable artificial intelligence. This approach recognizes that true intelligence emerges from the interplay between perception, action, and learning, rather than from purely computational processes.

The global reach of MIT's AI influence extends far beyond Cambridge, Massachusetts, as the institution actively shares its research findings and collaborates with international partners to address worldwide challenges. #include <stdbool>

int is_prime(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 0;
    if (n <= 3) return 1;
    if (n % 2 == 0 || n % 3 == 0) return 0;
    for (int i = 5; i * i <= n; i += 6) {
        if (n % i == 0 || n % (i + 2) == 0) return 0;
    }
    return 1;
}

Implement in C11: `int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str)`. Returns 1 if str matches the shell-style pattern pat, else 0. '*' matches any sequence (including empty), '?' matches exactly one character. All other characters match literally. The whole string must match.
Reply with only a C code block. No main function, no tests, no explanation.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str) {
    if (*pat == '\0') {
        return *str == '\0';
    }
    
    if (*(pat + 1) == '*') {
        if (glob_match(pat + 2, str)) {
            return 1;
        }
        if (*str != '\0' && (glob_match(pat, str + 1))) {
            return 1;
        }
        return 0;
    }
    
    if (*str == '\0') {
        return 0;
    }
    
    if (*pat == '?' || *pat == *str) {
        return glob_match(pat + 1, str + 1);
    }
    
    return 0;
}

double rpn_eval(const char *expr) {
    double stack[100];
    int top = -1;
    const char *token = strtok((char *)expr, " ");
    
    while (token) {
        if (isdigit(token[0])) {
            stack[++top] = atof(token);
        } else {
            double b = stack[top--];
            double a = stack[top--];
            switch (token[0]) {
                case '+': stack[++top] = a + b; break;
                case '-': stack[++top] = a - b; break;
                case '*': stack[++top] = a * b; break;
                case '/': stack[++top] = a / b; break;
            }
        }
        token = strtok(NULL, " ");
    }
    
    return stack[top];
}

#include <stddef.h>
#include <string.h>

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap) {
    if (idx < 0 || !line || !out || cap == 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    int field = 0;
    const char *p = line;
    size_t out_len = 0;

    while (*p) {
        if (*p == '"') {
            // Quoted field
            if (field == idx) {
                p++; // Skip opening quote
                while (*p) {
                    if (*p == '"') {
                        if (p[1] == '"') {
                            // Escaped quote
                            if (out_len < cap - 1) {
                                out[out_len++] = '"';
                            }
                            p++; // Skip next quote
                        } else {
                            // End of quoted field
                            break;
                        }
                    } else {
                        if (out_len < cap - 1) {
                            out[out_len++] = *p;
                        }
                    }
                    p++;
                }
                out[out_len] = '\0';
                return (int)out_len;
            } else {
                // Skip to end of quoted field
                p++;
                while (*p) {
                    if (*p == '"') {
                        if (p[1] == '"') {
                            p++;
                        } else {
                            break;
                        }
                    }
                    p++;
                }
                if (*p) p++; // Skip closing quote
                if (*p == ',') p++; // Skip comma
            }
        } else {
            // Unquoted field
            if (field == idx) {
                while (*p && *p != ',') {
                    if (out_len < cap - 1) {
                        out[out_len++] = *p;
                    }
                    p++;
                }
                out[out_len] = '\0';
                return (int)out_len;
            } else {
                while (*p && *p != ',') p++;
                if (*p == ',') p++;
            }
        }
        field++;
        if (*p == ',') p++;
    }

    // Handle last field without trailing comma
    if (field == idx) {
        if (out_len < cap - 1) {
            out[out_len] = '\0';
        }
        return (int)out_len;
    }

    return -1;
}

#include <string.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap) {
    if (idx < 0) return -1;
    
    int field_count = 0;
    const char *p = line;
    
    // Skip to the desired field
    while (*p && field_count < idx) {
        if (*p == '"') {
            // Quoted field
            p++;
            while (*p && *p != '"') p++;
            if (*p) p++; // Skip closing quote
            if (*p == '"') p++; // Skip doubled quote
        } else {
            // Unquoted field
            while (*p && *p != ',') p++;
        }
        if (*p == ',') p++;
        field_count++;
    }
    
    if (field_count != idx) return -1;
    
    if (!*p) return -1;
    
    size_t out_len = 0;
    
    if (*p == '"') {
        // Quoted field
        p++;
        while (*p && *p != '"') {
            if (out_len < cap - 1) out[out_len++] = *p;
            p++;
        }
        if (*p == '"') p++; // Skip closing quote
        // Handle doubled quotes
        while (*p == '"') {
            if (out_len < cap - 1) out[out_len++] = '"';
            p++;
            if (*p == '"') p++; // Skip next quote
        }
        if (*p == '"') p++; // Skip closing quote
    } else {
        // Unquoted field
        while (*p && *p != ',') {
            if (out_len < cap - 1) out[out_len++] = *p;
            p++;
        }
    }
    
    out[out_len] = '\0';
    return (int)out_len;
}

Returns a sorted list of dotted key paths where they differ: changed scalar/list values, keys present in only one side. Dicts are recursed into; lists and scalars are compared as whole values. Empty list means identical.
Reply with only a Python code block. No tests, no explanation.
trial 2 (temp 0.7) — fail — SyntaxError: 'elif' block follows an 'else' block
def json_diff(a, b, path=""):
    """
    Compares two JSON-like structures (dicts, lists, scalars).
    Returns a sorted list of dotted key paths where they differ.
    """
    differences = []
    
    # If both are dicts, compare recursively
    if isinstance(a, dict) and isinstance(b, dict):
        all_keys = set(a.keys()) | set(b.keys())
        for key in all_keys:
            new_path = f"{path}.{key}" if path else key
            if key not in a:
                # Key only in b
                differences.append(new_path)
            elif key not in b:
                # Key only in a
                differences.append(new_path)
            else:
                # Key in both, recurse
                differences.extend(json_diff(a[key], b[key], new_path))
    
    # If both are lists, compare as whole values
    elif isinstance(a, list) and isinstance(b, list):
        if a != b:
            differences.append(path)
    
    # If both are scalars, compare as whole values
    else:
        if a != b:
            differences.append(path)
    
    # One is dict, other is not
    elif isinstance(a, dict) or isinstance(b, dict):
        differences.append(path)
    
    # One is list, other is not
    elif isinstance(a, list) or isinstance(b, list):
        differences.append(path)
    
    return sorted(differences)

void arena_init(void *buf, size_t size); void *arena_alloc(size_t n); void arena_free(void *p); void *arena_realloc(void *p, size_t n);
arena_init hands the allocator a buffer and resets all state. void arena_init(void *buf, size_t size) {
    arena.buffer = buf;
    arena.buffer_size = size;

On success writes the code point to *cp and returns how many bytes it consumed (1-4). Returns -1 if the input is not strictly valid UTF-8, leaving *cp untouched. Strict means rejecting: overlong encodings (any code point not using its shortest form), UTF-16 surrogates U+D800-U+DFFF, anything above U+10FFFF, the obsolete 5- and 6-byte forms, a continuation byte in the leading position, bad continuation bytes, and sequences truncated by n. int utf8_next(const unsigned char *s, size_t n, uint32_t *cp) {
    if (n == 0) return -1;
    
    unsigned char byte = s[0];
    int len;
    uint32_t codepoint;
    
    if ((byte & 0x80) == 0) {
        len = 1;
        codepoint = byte;
    } else if ((byte & 0xE0) == 0xC0) {
        len = 2;
        codepoint = byte & 0x1F;
    } else if ((byte & 0xF0) == 0xE0) {
        len = 3;
        codepoint = byte & 0x0F;
    } else if ((byte & 0xF8) == 0xF0) {
        len = 4;
        codepoint = byte & 0x07;
    } else {
        return -1;
    }
    
    if (len > (int)n) return -1;
    
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        if ((s[i] & 0xC0) != 0x80) return -1;
        codepoint = (codepoint << 6) | (s[i] & 0x3F);
    }
    
    if (len == 2) {
        if (codepoint < 0x80) return -1;
    } else if (len == 3) {
        if (codepoint < 0x800) return -1;
        if (codepoint >= 0xD800 && codepoint <= 0xDFFF) return -1;
    } else if (len == 4) {
        if (codepoint < 0x10000) return -1;
        if (codepoint > 0x10FFFF) return -1;
    }
    
    *cp = codepoint;
    return len;
}

Implement in bash: `csv_to_tsv <file>`. Converts an RFC-4180 CSV file to TSV on stdout. Each CSV record becomes one output line, fields joined by a single tab. A field may be quoted with double quotes, in which case it can contain commas, tabs, line breaks, and the sequence "" meaning one literal double quote; the surrounding quotes are removed. Because a tab and a newline cannot appear literally in TSV, a line break inside a quoted field is written as the two characters backslash n, and a tab inside a field as the two characters backslash t. Line endings in the input may be CRLF or LF and the CR must not survive into the output. The last record may have no trailing newline; the output always ends with one. Empty fields stay empty. Python, Perl, Ruby, PHP and Node are not available.

    local file="$1"

    while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
        # Normalize line endings
        line="${line%$'\r'}"

        field=""
        quoted=0
        
        for ((i=0; i<${#line}; i++)); do
            char="${line:$i:1}"

                if [[ "$char" == '"' ]]; then
                    if [[ "${line:$((i+1)):1}" == '"' ]]; then

csv_to_tsv() {
    local file="$1"
    local line buffer field quoted value
    local IFS=','
    
    while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
        # Normalize line endings
        line="${line%$'\r'}"
        buffer=""
        
        while [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
            # Check if field is quoted
            if [[ "$line" == \"* ]]; then
                quoted=1
                line="${line:1}"  # Remove leading quote
                field=""
                
                while [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
                    if [[ "$line" == \"* ]]; then
                        # Check for escaped quote
                        if [[ "${line:1:1}" == "\"" ]]; then
                            field+="\"\"
                            line="${line:2}"
                        else
                            # End of quoted field
                            line="${line:1}"
                            break
                        fi
                    else
                        field+="${line:0:1}"
                        line="${line:1}"
                    fi
                done
                
                # Handle remaining line after quoted field
                if [[ -n "$line" && "$line" != ","* ]]; then
                    # Shouldn't happen in valid CSV, but handle gracefully
                    field+="$line"
                    line=""
                fi
                
                # Remove surrounding quotes and process escapes
                value="${field#\"}"
                value="${value%\"}"
                value="${value//\\n/\\n}"
                value="${value//\\t/\\t}"
                value="${value//\"\"/\"}"
            else
                # Unquoted field - take everything up to comma or end
                if [[ "$line" == *","* ]]; then
                    field="${line%%,*}"
                    line="${line#*,}"
                else
                    field="$line"
                    line=""
                fi
                value="$field"
            fi
            
            if [[ -n "$buffer" ]]; then
                buffer+=$'\t'
            fi
            buffer+="$value"
        done
        
        echo "$buffer"
    done < "$file"
}

csv_to_tsv() {
    local file="$1"
    local field=""
    local in_quotes=false
    local output_line=""
    local first_field=true
    local char=""
    local next_char=""
    local escaped_char=""
    
    while IFS= read -r -n1 char < "$file" || [[ -n "$char" ]]; do
        if $in_quotes; then
            if [[ "$char" == '"' ]]; then
                read -n1 next_char < "$file" 2>/dev/null || next_char=""
                if [[ "$next_char" == '"' ]]; then
                    field+='""'
                    continue
                else
                    in_quotes=false
                    if [[ -n "$next_char" ]]; then
                        char="$next_char"
                    else
                        char=""
                    fi
                fi
            elif [[ "$char" == $'\n' ]]; then
                field+='\\n'
                continue
            elif [[ "$char" == $'\t' ]]; then
                field+='\\t'
                continue
            else
                field+="$char"
                continue
            fi
        fi
        
        if [[ "$char" == '"' ]]; then
            in_quotes=true
            field=""
        elif [[ "$char" == ',' ]]; then
            if $first_field; then
                output_line="$field"
                first_field=false
            else
                output_line="$output_line"$'\t'"$field"
            fi
            field=""
        elif [[ "$char" == $'\r' ]]; then
            continue
        elif [[ "$char" == $'\n' ]]; then
            if $first_field; then
                output_line="$field"
            else
                output_line="$output_line"$'\t'"$field"
            fi
            echo "$output_line"
            output_line=""
            field=""
            first_field=true
        else
            field+="$char"
        fi
    done < "$file"
    
    if $first_field; then
        output_line="$field"
    else
        output_line="$output_line"$'\t'"$field"
    fi
    echo "$output_line"
}

Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) stands as a beacon of innovation and intellectual rigor, particularly in the realm of artificial intelligence (AI). Since its inception, MIT has been at the forefront of AI research, shaping the field with groundbreaking discoveries and fostering a culture of exploration and collaboration. The journey began in the mid-20th century when MIT became the birthplace of AI as a formal discipline. Pioneers like Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy laid the groundwork, establishing the field's theoretical foundations and setting the stage for future advancements. Minsky's work on perceptrons and McCarthy's introduction of the Lisp programming language were pivotal, providing the tools and concepts that would drive AI research for decades.

MIT's contributions to AI are vast and multifaceted, spanning key areas such as computer vision, natural language processing, robotics, machine learning, and neural networks. In computer vision, MIT researchers have developed algorithms that enable machines to interpret and understand visual data, revolutionizing fields like autonomous vehicles and medical imaging. In natural language processing, advancements like the development of the first AI programs capable of understanding human speech have transformed how we interact with technology. Robotics research at MIT has led to the creation of sophisticated systems capable of performing complex tasks, from disaster response to precision manufacturing.

Within MIT, institutions like the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) and the Media Lab have been instrumental in pushing the boundaries of AI. CSAIL has been a hub for cutting-edge research, contributing to breakthroughs in machine learning and neural networks. The Media Lab, with its interdisciplinary approach, has explored the intersection of technology and human experience, leading to innovations in AI that enhance creativity and accessibility. These institutions not only advance technical capabilities but also consider the ethical and societal implications of AI, ensuring that progress is both responsible and inclusive.

MIT's influence extends beyond its campus through its alumni, who have become leaders in various sectors. Notable figures such as Elon Musk, Bill Gates, and others have leveraged their MIT education to drive innovation in AI and related fields. Their contributions, from electric vehicles to software development, underscore MIT's role in nurturing talent that shapes industries and addresses global challenges.

Current research at MIT continues to explore emerging areas like deep learning, reinforcement learning, and ethical AI. Researchers are developing algorithms that enable machines to learn from experience and adapt to new situations, enhancing their ability to solve complex problems. Simultaneously, there is a growing emphasis on ethical considerations, ensuring that AI technologies are developed responsibly and equitably. This dual focus on innovation and ethics positions MIT as a leader in preparing for the future of AI.

Collaborations between MIT and industry, government, and other academic institutions further amplify its impact. These partnerships facilitate the translation of research into real-world applications, addressing challenges in healthcare, climate change, and urban planning. By bridging the gap between academia and practice, MIT ensures that its advancements benefit society at large.

In conclusion, MIT's enduring influence on AI research is a testament to its commitment to excellence and innovation. Through foundational work, cutting-edge research, and a focus on ethical development, MIT continues to shape the future of AI, addressing both the opportunities and challenges it presents. As the field evolves, MIT remains a driving force, inspiring the next generation of researchers and leaders to push the boundaries of what is possible.

import csv

def csv_column_sum(path, col):
    total = 0.0
    with open(path, 'r') as f:
        reader = csv.reader(f)
        next(reader)  # Skip the header

                try:

                    pass
    return total

    const char *ptr = line;
    int field = 0;
    size_t out_len = 0;
    bool in_quotes = false;
    
    while (*ptr != '\0') {
        if (field == idx) {
            while (*ptr != '\0') {
                if (in_quotes) {
                    if (*ptr == '"') {
                        ptr++;
                        if (*ptr == '"') {  // handle escaped quote
                            if (out_len < cap - 1) {
                                out[out_len++] = '"';
                            }
                            ptr++;
                        } else {
                            in_quotes = false;
                        }
                    } else {
                        if (out_len < cap - 1) {
                            out[out_len++] = *ptr;
                        }
                        ptr++;
                    }
                } else {
                    if (*ptr == ',') {
                        break;
                    } else if (*ptr == '"') {
                        in_quotes = true;
                        ptr++;
                    } else {
                        if (out_len < cap - 1) {
                            out[out_len++] = *ptr;
                        }
                        ptr++;
                    }
                }
            }
            out[out_len] = '\0';
            return out_len;
        }
        
        if (in_quotes) {
            if (*ptr == '"' && ptr[1] == '"') {  // skip escaped quote
                ptr += 2;
            } else if (*ptr == '"') {
                in_quotes = false;
                ptr++;
            } else {
                ptr++;
            }
        } else {
            if (*ptr == '"') {
                in_quotes = true;
                ptr++;
            } else if (*ptr == ',') {
                field++;
                ptr++;
            } else {
                ptr++;
            }
        }
    }
    
    if (field == idx && *ptr == '\0') {
        out[0] = '\0';
        return 0;
    }
    
    return -1;
}

To solve this problem, we need to implement a topological sort function that takes a dictionary of dependencies and returns a list of nodes in an order where each node comes after its dependencies. If there is a cycle in the graph, the function should return `None`.

### Approach
The approach we use is based on Kahn's algorithm, which is efficient for topological sorting and also helps in detecting cycles in the graph. Here are the steps involved:

1. **Collect All Nodes**: Extract all unique nodes from the given dependencies. This includes nodes that are only mentioned as dependencies and not as keys in the dictionary.

2. **Build Adjacency List and In-Degree Count**: Construct an adjacency list to represent the graph and an in-degree count for each node. The adjacency list helps in tracking the neighbors of each node, while the in-degree count helps in determining when a node can be processed.

3. **Initialize Queue with Zero In-Degree Nodes**: Start with nodes that have zero in-degree, as these nodes have no dependencies and can be processed first.

4. **Process Nodes Using Queue**: Use a queue to process each node. For each node processed, add it to the result list and decrement the in-degree count of its neighbors. If any neighbor's in-degree becomes zero, enqueue it.

5. **Check for Cycles**: After processing all nodes, if the result list does not contain all nodes, it indicates a cycle in the graph, and we return `None`.

### Solution Code

from collections import deque

def topological_sort(deps):
    if not deps:
        return []
    
    all_nodes = set(deps.keys())
    for deps_list in deps.values():
        all_nodes.update(deps_list)
    all_nodes = list(all_nodes)
    
    in_degree = {node: 0 for node in all_nodes}
    adj = {node: [] for node in all_nodes}
    
    for u in deps:
        for v in deps[u]:
            adj[v].append(u)
            in_degree[u] += 1
    
    queue = deque()
    for node in all_nodes:
        if in_degree[node] == 0:
            queue.append(node)
    
    result = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        result.append(node)
        for neighbor in adj[node]:
            in_degree[neighbor] -=

#include <string.h>

void trim(char *s) {
    if (!s) return;
    // Find first non-whitespace character
    char *start = s;
    while (*start && (*start == ' ' || *start == '\t' || *start == '\n')) {
        ++start;
    }
    // Find last non-whitespace character
    char *end = s + strlen(s) - 1;
    while (end > start && (*end == ' ' || *end == '\t' || *end == '\n')) {
        --end;
    }
    // Shift characters to overwrite leading whitespace
    char *dst = start;
    while (*end) {
        *dst++ = *end++;
    }
    *dst = '\0';
}

#include <string.h>
#include <ctype.h>

void trim(char *s) {
    if (!s) return;
    size_t len = strlen(s);
    size_t start = 0;
    while (start < len && isspace((unsigned char)s[start]))
        ++start;
    size_t end = len;
    while (end > start && isspace((unsigned char)s[end - 1]))
        --end;
    if (start == 0 && end == len)
        return;
    memmove(s, s + start, end - start + 1);
}

#include <stddef.h>

typedef struct {
    int data[8];
    int head;
    int count;
} Ring;

void ring_init(Ring *r) {
    if (!r) return;
    r->head = 0;
    r->count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {
        r->data[i] = 0;
    }
}

int ring_push(Ring *r, int v) {
    if (!r) return -1;
    if (r->count == 8) {
        return -1;
    }
    int idx = (r->head + r->count) % 8;
    r->data[idx] = v;
    r->count++;
    return 0;
}

int ring_pop(Ring *r, int *out) {
    if (!r || !out) return -1;
    if (r->count == 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    *out = r->data[r->head];
    r->head = (r->head + 1) % 8;
    r->count--;
    return 0;

def is_valid_ipv4(s):
    parts = s.split('.')
    if len(parts) != 4:
        return False
    for part in parts:

- **NFS over TLS support (new feature)** – RHEL 10 now provides full TLS encryption for NFS RPC traffic, relying on kernel TLS (kTLS) (Technology Preview). This change enhances security by encrypting client‑server communication, but it may add encryption overhead that can affect performance; administrators can weigh the security benefit against any latency impact.

- **IPv6 address handling in nfs:// URLs (bug fix)** – The parsing of IPv6 addresses enclosed in square brackets (e.g., `nfs://[2001:db8::1]/`) was broken, causing ReaR to abort with “Invalid scheme”. The fix correctly interprets the brackets, allowing IPv6 addresses in BACKUP_URL/OUTPUT_URL without requiring backslashes. This restores usability and prevents premature failures when using IPv6‑addressed NFS servers.

- **Client‑side NFS caching via FS‑Cache (new performance feature)** – A new mount option enables NFS shares to be cached locally using the FS‑Cache framework (backed by `cachefilesd`). Cached reads are served from the client’s local storage, dramatically reducing network traffic and server load. The feature can improve overall NFS client performance for frequently accessed data, though it may add CPU/memory overhead for cache management.

- **`vers` mount option clarified (compatibility fix)** – The `vers` option is now documented as identical to `nfsvers`, ensuring consistent behavior across tools and reducing configuration errors. While it does not change performance, it simplifies correct version selection, helping administrators avoid mis‑configured mounts that could lead to suboptimal performance.

- **cachefilesd service prerequisites updated (performance enablement)** – Documentation now specifies that the cache back‑end must be an `ext3`, `ext4`, or `xfs` file system mounted at `/var/cache/fscache/` with extended attributes (default on RHEL 8+). This ensures the caching infrastructure works correctly, allowing the new FS‑Cache NFS feature to deliver its performance benefits.

- **NFS with TLS support** – RHEL 10 now offers fully‑supported NFS over TLS (using kernel TLS). - **IPv6 address handling in nfs:// URLs** – Fixed a bug where IPv6 addresses in `nfs://` or `sshfs://` URLs had to be escaped with backslashes. The update correctly interprets bracketed IPv6 addresses (e.g., `nfs://[2001:db8::101]/...`), allowing clients to specify IPv6 endpoints directly in `BACKUP_URL`/`OUTPUT_URL` without work‑arounds, improving usability and reliability for IPv6‑based NFS deployments.  

- **Client‑side caching for NFS via FS‑Cache** – Introduced NFS client‑side caching using the `cachefilesd` daemon and the `cachefiles` back‑end. - **NFS with TLS support (Technology Preview)** – RHEL 10 now fully supports NFS over TLS, using kernel TLS (kTLS) to encrypt RPC traffic. This adds a security layer for NFS server/client communication, enabling secure deployments while noting that kTLS is still a preview feature and may impact performance due to encryption overhead.  

- **IPv6 address parsing fix for nfs:// URLs** – A bug in ReaR caused nfs:// and sshfs:// URLs containing IPv6 addresses in brackets (e.g., `nfs://[2001:db8::1]/`) to abort with “Invalid scheme”. The fix ensures brackets are correctly interpreted, allowing IPv6 hosts to be used as NFS servers in BACKUP_URL/OUTPUT_URL. This restores reliability for IPv6‑based NFS client configurations.  

- **Client‑side NFS caching via FS‑Cache (cachefilesd)** – RHEL 10 introduces native NFS client caching that leverages the `cachefiles` back‑end and the `cachefilesd` daemon. By mounting an NFS share with the caching option, read operations are served locally, dramatically reducing network traffic and server load while improving response times. The feature is configurable through `/etc/cachefilesd.conf` and requires an ext3/4 or XFS cache device with extended attributes, providing a tunable performance boost for NFS workloads.

• **ReaR `nfs://` URL IPv6 parsing fix (Excerpt 3):** ReaR previously misinterpreted the square brackets around an IPv6 address in an `nfs://` (or `sshfs://`) URL as shell metacharacters, causing `BACKUP_URL`/`OUTPUT_URL` to abort with an "Invalid scheme" error. The parser was corrected so that `nfs://[2001:db8::…]/path` works natively. This matters because it removes a blocking bug for anyone backing up over NFS to an IPv6-only server and eliminates the need for the fragile backslash-quoting workaround.

• **`rsize` / `wsize` maximum of 1 048 576 bytes in RHEL 10 (Excerpt 4):** The documentation explicitly states that in RHEL 10 the client and server maximum for a single NFS read or write operation is 1 MB. This matters for throughput tuning: administrators can now size I/O to the full 1 MB ceiling (up from lower historical maxima on older releases), reducing the number of round-trips per transfer and improving large-file performance over TCP.

• **FS-Cache / `cachefilesd` client-side NFS caching (Excerpt 5):** RHEL 10 continues to provide the `cachefiles` back-end (via the `cachefilesd` daemon and the `cachefiles` kernel module) so that an NFS client can persistently cache file data on a local XFS, ext3, or ext4 volume under `/var/cache/fscache/`. This matters for performance because read requests are satisfied from local disk instead of the network, reducing both network bandwidth consumption and server load; the trade-off is a potential slight slowdown on the client side when cache misses or coherency checks occur.

the establishment of the MIT AI Laboratory in 1959, spearheaded by Minsky and McCarthy, was a pivotal moment, creating the world's first dedicated research center for AI, a physical and intellectual hub that attracted brilliant minds and fostered an environment where theoretical exploration and practical experimentation could coexist and thrive, fundamentally differentiating MIT's approach from more isolated academic pursuits elsewhere, and this lab, later evolving into the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) in 2003, became the crucible for countless seminal ideas; early work at MIT focused on symbolic reasoning and problem-solving, exemplified by the Logic Theorist, developed by Allen Newell and Herbert Simon (though Simon was at Carnegie Mellon, the project was deeply influenced by the broader AI community centered at MIT), and the General Problem Solver, but MIT's unique contribution lay in its embrace of diverse approaches, including the pioneering work on neural networks; the AI winter of the 1970s and 1980s, a period of reduced funding and interest following the initial hype, saw MIT researchers not merely weathering the storm but actively redefining the field, shifting focus towards more robust, knowledge-based systems and the practical application of AI techniques, with Minsky's work on frame theory and the development of the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory's focus on "common sense" reasoning and expert systems laying groundwork for later advancements, while the lab also became a critical training ground for generations of AI researchers, including future leaders like Rodney Brooks, who would later found Rethink Robotics and pioneer the "subsumption architecture" for robotics, a departure from purely symbolic AI that emphasized reactive, behavior-based systems; - NFS client now correctly handles IPv6 addresses in `nfs://` URLs (e.g., `nfs://[2001:db8::1]`), resolving a bug that previously caused mount failures and required workarounds like escaping brackets. This matters for clients using IPv6-based NFS servers without manual configuration.  
- Default `rsize` and `wsize` values increased to 1,048,576 bytes (1 MB), improving NFS transfer efficiency by reducing network round trips per operation. This matters as larger block sizes enhance throughput for both client and server performance.

- **Fixed ReaR handling of IPv6 addresses in NFS URLs** (Excerpt 3): Previously, using IPv6 addresses (e.g., `nfs://[2001:db8:ca2:6::101]/`) in `BACKUP_URL`/`OUTPUT_URL` caused ReaR to abort due to incorrect bracket interpretation. Now correctly parses brackets, enabling IPv6-based NFS mounts without workarounds. *Matters because it resolves a critical failure point for IPv6 NFS deployments in backup workflows.*
- **Added client-side caching via FS-Cache for NFS** (Excerpt 5): Enables transparent client-side caching using `cachefilesd` (with XFS/ext4/xfs backends) to reduce network traffic and server load by serving reads from local cache. *Matters because it directly improves NFS client performance and reduces server load for frequently accessed data.*

#include <stddef.h>

typedef struct {
    int data[16];
    int top;
} Stack;

void stack_init(Stack *s) {
    s->top = 16;
}

int stack_push(Stack *s, int v) {
    if (s->top == 16) {
        return -1;
    }
    s->data[--s->top] = v;
    return 0;
}

int stack_pop(Stack *s, int *out) {
    if (s->top == 16) {
        return -1;
    }
    *out = s->data[s->top++];
    return 0;
}
